Our study has several limitations.

**#1（强烈推荐）：Tail-truncation budget curve（候选1）**

- 这是论文最具视觉冲击力的发现——384→512 token 的 phase transition，4 模型同时跳变 13-22pp。审稿人一眼就能记住。

- 直接支撑论文核心贡献 #3（practical fallback recommendation: ≥512 tokens）和 Discussion 的"implicit pathway"论点。
- 跨架构一致性（4 模型同时跳变）在图上一目了然，文字很难传达这种"齐刷刷的同步性"。
- Appendix 已有数据（fig:trace_length / budget_curve），搬到正文成本低。

Design spec：
- 尺寸：column-width（\columnwidth），约占 1/3 page
- 布局：单面板折线图，x 轴 = tail token budget（256, 384, 512, 1024, 2048），y 轴 = accuracy (%)
- 4 条线（Qwen-7B, Qwen-1.5B, CodeLlama-13B, DeepSeek-6.7B），颜色区分
- 标注 384→512 区间为灰色 shaded "phase transition zone"
- 虚线标注 exception_only ceiling（~99.5%）和 no_trace floor（~73%）作为参考
- Insight：所有模型在同一 token 阈值处同步跳变，证明信号位置是结构性的（globals module dump boundary ~384 tokens），不是模型依赖的

**#2（推荐）：Training dynamics（候选2）**

理由：
- 支撑论文的因果论证：为什么 full_trace 差？不是因为训练 loss 不收敛（loss 确实在降），而是准确率不收敛——exception_only 50 步到 99.83% 而 full_trace 持续震荡。
- Discussion 段已引用这个 figure 作为 content quality 论点的佐证。
- 视觉上清晰：两条线的鲜明对比，无需解释就能看懂。

- 尺寸：column-width，约 1/3 page
- 布局：双 y 轴或单面板。x 轴 = training step, y 轴 = eval accuracy (%)

The gap concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases: regex flags all exception events as failures, while SFT learns to distinguish caught exceptions (benign, inside \texttt{try/except}) from uncaught faults, correctly resolving 6/8 boundary samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Across all formats, SFT outperforms the best applicable regex by +3.62--23.86pp (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).

\paragraph{Zero-shot and few-shot LLM baselines.}
Zero-shot prompting spans 51.0--93.5\% across four models (42.44pp range); three-shot ICL on Qwen-7B (90.84\%) improves only 1.76pp.
SFT compresses this range to 0.50pp (99.39--99.89\%), closing a 6--49pp gap with 4,720 samples (Appendix~\ref{sec:zeroshot_cross_model}).
\paragraph{Frontier model crossover.}
Two frontier models illustrate that SFT's advantage depends on input density: under \texttt{no\_trace}, GPT-4o (84.45\%) and GPT-4.1 (77.31\%) outperform SFT Qwen-7B (75.13\%), but under \texttt{exception\_only} the ranking reverses (SFT 99.83\% vs.\ GPT-4o 87.98\%).
Compact diagnostic input unlocks SFT's full advantage over general reasoning capacity.

\subsection{Format Marker Ablation}
\label{sec:nomarker}

The \texttt{exception\_only} format includes a \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} marker in all pass-class samples (regex baseline B5 exploits this for 99.33\% accuracy; Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
To quantify the marker's contribution, we retrain with all format markers removed (\texttt{nomarker} condition).

Qwen-7B 3-seed mean: 97.65\% $\pm$ 0.96 (seeds 42/123/456: 96.55/98.32/98.07\%), a drop of 2.18pp from \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%).
Qwen-1.5B: 97.82\%, drop of 2.01pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$2pp) accounts for only ${\sim}$9\% of the total exception lift over \texttt{no\_trace} (24.70pp on 7B).
Regex baselines illustrate this decomposition: B5 (\texttt{[No exception data]}$\to$pass, 99.33\% with markers) collapses to 28.49\% without markers, showing it is entirely format-dependent.
The strongest semantic regex B4 (exception class matching, 93.61\%) is marker-invariant; SFT \texttt{nomarker} (97.65\%) exceeds it by 4.04pp, isolating the learned semantic contribution beyond pattern matching.

\paragraph{Cross-dataset transfer.}
Bidirectional evaluation demonstrates generalization: HumanEval${\to}$MBPP \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.41\% ($N{=}4{,}270$) and MBPP${\to}$HumanEval achieves 100.0\% ($N{=}1{,}640$), while \texttt{no\_trace} drops to near-majority baseline in both directions (70.56\% vs.\ 69.02\% majority; 67.99\% vs.\ 61.65\%).
The near-zero transfer loss for exception signals, across independently authored problem sets with no problem overlap, shows SFT learns language-level diagnostic patterns, not dataset-specific artifacts.
Under marker removal, cross-dataset accuracy drops to 95.5\% ($-$3.9pp), indicating that the majority of cross-dataset transfer relies on learned diagnostic patterns rather than format markers.

\subsection{Decomposing the Full-Trace Degradation}
\label{sec:density}

The 18.07pp gap between \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) and \texttt{full\_trace} (81.76\%) could reflect gradient dilution (diagnostic tokens are ${\sim}$1/500 of full traces, diluting gradient signal during training) or content quality (verbose input buries diagnostic signals at inference).

\paragraph{Controlled gradient masking.}
To isolate gradient dilution, we mask 99.8\% of gradient updates during \texttt{exception\_only} training, matching the diagnostic token ratio of full traces while preserving compact input.
This yields 99.22\% (mean $-$0.61pp from \texttt{exception\_only}, 3 seeds), limiting gradient dilution to ${\leq}$4\% of the 18.07pp gap (Table~\ref{tab:density}).
The gradient masking bound attributes the remaining ${\geq}$96\% to content quality (diagnostic signal density at inference), though forward-pass attention during masked training is an unquantified residual.
Note that masking affects only the backward pass; the model still attends to all input tokens during the forward pass, so this bounds gradient dilution's contribution but does not rule out attention-based information flow as a residual confound.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Decomposition of the full-trace degradation (Qwen-7B). Gradient masking attributes ${\leq}$4\% to gradient dilution; the bound assigns the remainder to content quality, though forward-pass attention is a residual confound (\S\ref{sec:density}). Label-only loss provides a confounded but directionally consistent complementary estimate.}
\label{tab:density}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{Acc (\%)} & \textbf{$\Delta$} \\
\midrule
exception\_only & 99.83{\scriptsize$\pm$0.00} & --- \\
\quad + grad mask (99.8\%) & 99.22{\scriptsize$\pm$0.20}$^\S$ & $-$0.61pp \\
full\_trace & 81.76$^\ddag$ & $-$18.07pp \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Complementary (confounded):}} \\
full\_trace + label-only loss & 85.94{\scriptsize$\pm$1.12} & +4.50pp$^\dag$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{2pt}
\par\raggedright\footnotesize
$^\S$Mean $\pm$ std over 3 seeds (42, 123, 456).
$^\ddag$Matched-seed baseline; 3-seed mean 81.44\%$\pm$1.11 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
$^\dag$vs.\ \texttt{full\_trace} (81.44\%$\pm$1.11); not significant under clustered bootstrap (95\% CI [$-$0.6, +9.8]pp, $n_\text{eff}{=}119$).
\end{table}

\paragraph{Complementary evidence.}
Label-only loss on full traces (+4.50pp, 3 seeds) yields a confounded upper bound of ${\leq}$26\% gradient contribution, consistent with the masking estimate (${\leq}$4\%) but not significant under clustered bootstrap (95\% CI [$-$0.6, +9.8]pp).
Qwen-1.5B shows a similar label-only pattern (17\%/83\%, 3 seeds); CodeLlama and DeepSeek exhibit label-only collapse to majority baseline (28.5\%), limiting this complementary analysis to the Qwen family.
The architecture dependence suggests label-only training is sensitive to model capacity or optimization landscape; the gradient masking ablation provides a more robust, architecture-independent decomposition.
Cross-architecture validation confirms this bound on two additional families: DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B achieves 99.33\% under 99.8\% masking (${\leq}$0.3\% dilution) and CodeLlama-13B achieves 100\% (dilution ${\leq}$0\%), consistent with the Qwen-7B result across all three architecture families.
Error analysis supports the content quality interpretation: all 217 \texttt{full\_trace} errors occur where tokenizer truncation removes diagnostic markers, manifesting through mechanical truncation rather than semantic confusion.

\subsection{Complementary Analyses}
\label{sec:additional}

\paragraph{Trace length ablation.}
\label{sec:trace_length}
Varying the head-truncated trace token budget (256--no limit) on Qwen-7B yields accuracy in a narrow 77.2\%--81.8\% band with a non-monotonic pattern: 1024-token prefixes (77.23\%) underperform 512-token prefixes (80.42\%, $p{=}.002$), because mid-length prefixes retain enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events near the trace terminus (Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}).
Critically, removing the token budget entirely (no truncation) yields 81.76\%, identical to head-2048, ruling out truncation as the explanation for the full-trace degradation.
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation; under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for two of three models (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model} in Appendix), with only DeepSeek showing a mild architecture-specific reversal at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048 ($-$1.5pp).

\paragraph{Truncation direction and budget curve.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: among the three models with complete data, tail-2048 exceeds head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp, with the gap widening at smaller scale (Qwen-1.5B: +22.6pp vs.\ Qwen-7B: +15.5pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:trace_length_full}, Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail}).
All four models' head-2048 accuracies converge into a narrow 75.3--81.8\% band (6.5pp), comparable to the tail-256 band (72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp), indicating that signal-poor conditions produce a shared performance floor regardless of scale or architecture.

A cross-model budget sweep across four models and three architecture families reveals a sharp performance jump localized between 384 and 512 tail tokens.
At tail-384, all models remain near baseline (73.6--80.7\%, only +1.0--4.8pp over tail-256); the steep jump occurs at 384$\to$512 (+13.2--22.0pp), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling (${\sim}$94--98\%).
This localizes the critical threshold to ${\sim}$400--500 tokens, crossing the globals module dump threshold (${\sim}$384 tokens) and exposing structured execution markers (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}).
CodeLlama tail conditions use label-only loss (\S\ref{sec:density}), which may inflate its tail accuracies; cross-model tail comparisons should account for this training difference.
Beyond 512 tokens, accuracy converges further: multi-seed validation across all 12 model$\times$seed combinations shows all tail-512 accuracies fall within a 4.63pp band [93.61\%, 98.24\%] (Table~\ref{tab:tail512_seeds}); at tail-1024, three models reach 96.5--98.2\%, compressing the 6.3pp cross-model spread observed at tail-256.
\texttt{tail\_2048} captures 95--98\% of \texttt{exception\_only}'s accuracy across all completed configurations.
The residual 2--5pp gap indicates that semantic extraction (identifying exception type and message) still outperforms positional extraction (retaining a fixed window containing non-diagnostic lines).

\paragraph{Calibration.}
\label{sec:calibration}
Calibration mirrors the tier hierarchy: \texttt{exception\_only} achieves ECE = 0.0027 vs.\ 0.171 for \texttt{no\_trace}, a 63$\times$ gap (Figure~\ref{fig:calibration}).
This calibration advantage generalizes across architectures and scales: all four models (1.5B--13B) achieve ECE ${<}$ 0.007 under \texttt{exception\_only} (Table~\ref{tab:calibration_model_level} in Appendix), indicating well-calibrated predictions rather than overfit confidence.

\paragraph{Error analysis.}
\texttt{exception\_only}'s 2 errors have zero overlap with all other conditions' error sets (Jaccard = 0.000; Appendix~\ref{sec:error_overlap}); per-type breakdown shows all standard exception types achieve 100\% accuracy, with only \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a benign \texttt{BaseException} subclass) causing failures (Appendix~\ref{sec:exception_type}).

\paragraph{Length control.}
Padding \texttt{exception\_only} to 2{,}048 tokens, even in a semantically loaded position (after the verdict region), yields identical accuracy (99.83\%), indicating the 18--23pp gap arises from spurious patterns in verbose trace content, not sequence length.

\paragraph{Supplementary OOD analysis.}
\label{sec:debugbench}
On DebugBench \citep{tian2024debugbench} ($N{=}426$), the condition ranking is preserved: \texttt{exception\_only} 100\%, VOTA 99.77\%, \texttt{no\_trace} 96.71\%.
However, narrow margins (3.29pp headroom from \texttt{no\_trace}) limit discriminative power; this supplementary analysis preserves the ranking but cannot establish effect sizes comparable to the primary dataset (Appendix~\ref{sec:debugbench_full}).
